newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Jerusalem's hardline mayor charged in funding case.
newsitem.headline: Jerusalem's hardline mayor charged in funding case.

text.p: Israeli prosecutors filed charges on Thursday against Jerusalem Mayor Ehud Olmert, a leading figure in Israel's ruling right-wing Likud party, in connection with an alleged 1988 campaign funding scam.
Court spokesman Moshe Gorali confirmed prosecutors filed charges against Olmert in Tel Aviv District Court on Thursday.

A charge sheet obtained by Reuters said Olmert "intentionally misled the State Comptroller" by "hiding the fact that the Likud received, against the provisions of the Campaign Funding Law, contributions from Israeli corporations."
It alleged then-party treasurer Olmert and other Likud financial officers created a fictitious public relations firm to receive and disguise donations from corporations.
Israeli election laws bar direct or indirect corporate contributions to political parties.
The charges do not accuse Olmert of reaping personal financial gain from the contributions.
A close political ally of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Olmert has long been under investigation over the allegations.

Political commentators have said Olmert, a senior minister and high-profile government spokesman during the former Likud administration of Yitzhak Shamir, was denied a cabinet post by Netanyahu over the alleged illegal funding affair.
The prosecution submitted a list of more than 100 witnesses it expected to call during the trial, among them two former Likud cabinet ministers.
Olmert, 51, won prominence in November, 1993, in an upset victory over octogenarian Teddy Kollek, who had been mayor of the volatile holy city for more than 27 years.
Throughout the years-long investigation, Olmert has consistently maintained he is innocent of any wrongdoing.
In the past, trials of public figures on corruption or fraud charges have commonly lasted for several years.
State-run Israel Television's Channel One quoted Olmert as rejecting calls by opposition lawmakers for the mayor to remove himself from office for the duration of the trial.
"I have no intention of suspending myself, there is no legal reason, public justification, no precedent for doing so," he said.
Legal authority Moshe Negbi said Israeli law was unclear on the suspension issue for mayors charged with crimes. He said the Supreme Court might be asked to rule on the question.
